headline: High: Flowise can write shared files and browse web content while pdf.js processes PDFs, creating default-path prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-error risks.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Flowise can read/write the server filesystem and run browsers, so attacker-controlled PDF content handled by pdf.js can be bridged into Flowise flows if operators connect them through files. pdf.js is file-based and browser-based, so the interaction is plausible, but not proven by docs alone. Shared workspace makes injection feasible.
conditions: IF pdf.js output or extracted text is copied into a Flowise prompt or file input
IF both agents share the same filesystem or uploaded-file directory
mitigations: Separate the agents into different workspaces
Disable automatic ingestion of extracted PDF text into Flowise prompts
Add a manual review step before any file-to-prompt transfer
Use read-only mounts for pdf.js outputs
requires-engineering: add provenance tags to all transferred content

B_data_leakage.rationale: Flowise touches chatflow inputs/outputs and model provider keys, and can access server filesystem and uploaded files. pdf.js processes PDF documents and files. If they share a workspace, sensitive PDF contents can flow into Flowise and then to model providers or tools. The pairwise leakage path is plausible in default deployments with shared storage.
conditions: IF PDF files in pdf.js are stored in the same directory Flowise can read
IF Flowise sends those contents to a model provider or HTTP tool
mitigations: Store PDFs outside Flowise-readable paths
Turn off automatic file attachment to prompts
Restrict Flowise tool credentials to non-sensitive scopes
Delete temporary PDF exports after processing
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Flowise has write_filesystem and broad network egress, while pdf.js has browser execution and file access but no network egress. They do not both show unrestricted write to the same mutable resource, so direct conflict is limited. The main overlap is file handling, which is manageable if storage is separated.
conditions: IF both agents are configured to write into the same directory
IF an orchestrator does not serialize file updates
mitigations: Assign separate output directories
Make pdf.js outputs read-only to Flowise
Avoid concurrent writes to shared files
Use per-run temp folders
requires-engineering: add locking around shared mutable paths

D_cascading_error.rationale: Flowise can act on chatflow outputs and call model providers or HTTP tools, so if it consumes pdf.js-derived text without verification, errors can cascade into downstream actions. pdf.js is a document processor, not a verifier, so its extracted content may be treated as authoritative by Flowise unless operators add checks. This is a default-path risk when chaining them.
conditions: IF Flowise uses pdf.js extraction as prompt context or tool input
IF no human or automated verification step checks the extracted text
mitigations: Insert a validation step before downstream actions
Require human approval for any action based on PDF extraction
Compare extracted text against the source PDF for critical fields
Limit Flowise to read-only summarization
requires-engineering: add confidence gating on extracted facts

E_compliance.rationale: Both agents are open-source and docs-only, and the profiles do not show a residency or certification mismatch. The only compliance-relevant data classes are chatflow inputs/outputs and PDF documents, so no specific breach pathway is evidenced. I do not cite only one agent because the pairwise compliance question is about mismatch, which is absent here.
conditions: IF a deployment routes regulated PDFs into a jurisdictionally restricted Flowise instance
IF retention policies differ between the shared storage layers
mitigations: Document data-class handling for both agents
Keep regulated PDFs out of shared workspaces
Align retention settings across storage layers
Review deployment residency before enabling production use
